header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
61: | `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
62: | `fix` | what to change. |
63: | `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
64: 
65: ## Checking your own work before you commit
66: 
67: ```sh
68: node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
69: ```
70: 
71: That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
72: 
73: ## What the integration delivers
74: 
75: The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.
76: 
77: `findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
78: 
79: ```sh
80: for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
81: ```
82: 
83: Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
84: 
85: `SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
86: 
87: ```markdown
88: ## Résumé exécutif
89: 
90: <deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
91: 
92: - critical: 0
93: - high: 0
94: - medium: 0
95: - low: 0
96: - info: 0
97: 
98: ## Executive summary
99: 
100: <the same in English>
101: 
102: - critical: 0
103: - high: 0
104: - medium: 0
105: - low: 0
106: - info: 0
107: 
108: ## Scope and method
109: 
110: <the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
111: 
112: ## Findings
113: 
114: ### critical
115: 
116: - `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>
117: 
118: ### high
119: 
120: ...
121: 
122: ## What was not covered
123: 
124: - <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
125: - <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
126: 
127: ## Certificate
128: 
129: Verified findings: <count>
130: Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>
131: 
132: <one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>
133: 
134: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
135: ```
136: 
137: Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.
138: 
139: The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.
140: 
141: Check it before you commit:
142: 
143: ```sh
144: node verify-safety-report.mjs --report
145: ```

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: // Mechanical examiner of a code-safety report. It is in the report
3: // repository's base commit, so no department can change what measures it.
4: //
5: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path>  one department's findings
6: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path> --list-invalid
7: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --report           the merged report
8: //
9: // `--findings` decides one findings file against the target tree. Adding
10: // `--list-invalid` turns the same decision into a report: the failing ids go to
11: // stdout, one per line, and the exit code is 0, which is how the integration
12: // learns which findings to drop and disclose.
13: //
14: // `--report` decides SAFETY-REPORT.md and findings.json together, including the
15: // disclosure rule: every id any `findings/<department>.json` carries and
16: // findings.json does not must be named under `## What was not covered`.
17: //
18: // Exit 0 only when every rule holds; otherwise every failure is printed to
19: // stderr, one per line, and the exit code is 1. Node built-ins only, because

34:   '## Executive summary',
35:   '## Scope and method',
36:   '## Findings',

42: const HONESTY = 'This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".'
43: 
44: /** Claims no coverage this review can state would support. */
45: const OVERCLAIMS = /\bno vulnerabilities\b|\bfree of vulnerabilities\b|\b(?:is|are|was|were) secure\b|\bsafe to deploy\b|\bproven secure\b|\bfully audited\b/i

59: /**
60:  * Every file under one directory, relative and sorted, skipping the excluded names.
61:  * @param {string} root directory to walk
62:  * @param {string[]} exclude directory basenames never descended into
63:  * @returns {string[]} relative POSIX-ish paths, sorted
64:  */
65: function walk(root, exclude) {
66:   const found = []
67:   const descend = (directory) => {
68:     for (const entry of readdirSync(directory, { withFileTypes: true }).sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))) {
69:       const path = join(directory, entry.name)
70:       if (entry.isDirectory()) {
71:         if (!exclude.includes(entry.name)) descend(path)
72:       } else if (entry.isFile()) found.push(relative(root, path))
73:     }
74:   }
75:   descend(root)

79: /** One target tree as the lock and the verifier both read it: the files, their digests, and their text. */
80: class Target {
81:   /**
82:    * @param {string} reportRoot the report repository the lock is committed in
83:    * @param {string[]} failures collector every rule appends to
84:    */

86:     this.failures = failures

91:     if (!existsSync(lockPath)) {
92:       failures.push('target.json is missing from this worktree; the base commit carries the lock of the tree under review')
93:       return
94:     }
95:     const lock = JSON.parse(readFileSync(lockPath, 'utf8'))
96:     this.root = lock.root
97:     this.exclude = lock.exclude ?? []
98:     this.digest = lock.sha256
99:     for (const [path, hash] of Object.entries(lock.files)) this.files.set(path, hash)
100:     this.checkTree()

103:   /**
104:    * Refuse a target that changed since the base commit locked it: a finding
105:    * cites a line of the tree this program was asked to review, and a tree a
106:    * department edited is no longer that tree.
107:    */
108:   checkTree() {
109:     if (!existsSync(this.root)) {
110:       this.failures.push(`the target tree ${this.root} is not on this host, so no citation can be resolved`)
111:       this.root = undefined
112:       return
113:     }
114:     const present = walk(this.root, this.exclude)
115:     for (const path of present) {
116:       if (!this.files.has(path)) this.failures.push(`the target tree gained ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
117:     }
118:     for (const [path, hash] of this.files) {
119:       if (!present.includes(path)) {
120:         this.failures.push(`the target tree lost ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
121:         continue
122:       }
123:       if (sha256(readFileSync(join(this.root, path))) !== hash) {
124:         this.failures.push(`the target tree's ${path} changed since the base commit locked it; the target is read-only for this program`)

127:   }

129:   /**
130:    * The lines of one target file.

132:    * @returns {string[] | undefined} the file's lines, or undefined when it is not in the locked tree
133:    */
134:   linesOf(path) {
135:     if (this.root === undefined || !this.files.has(path)) return undefined

140:   /**
141:    * Whether one `file:line` citation resolves in the locked tree.
142:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
143:    * @param {number} line 1-based line number
144:    * @returns {boolean} whether the file is under review and holds that line
145:    */
146:   resolves(path, line) {
147:     const lines = this.linesOf(path)
148:     return lines !== undefined && Number.isInteger(line) && line >= 1 && line <= lines.length

152: /**
153:  * Decide one finding against the target tree.
154:  * @param {unknown} finding one entry of a findings file
155:  * @param {number} index its position, named when the entry has no usable id
156:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree the finding cites
157:  * @param {Set<string>} seen ids already used in this file
158:  * @returns {string[]} every rule this finding broke, empty when it holds
159:  */
160: function checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen) {
161:   const failures = []
162:   if (finding === null || typeof finding !== 'object' || Array.isArray(finding)) {
163:     return [`finding #${index + 1} is not a JSON object`]

169:   // numbering the knowledge pack's schema uses and a department-prefixed name.
170:   if (typeof id !== 'string' || !/^[A-Za-z0-9][\w.-]*$/.test(id)) fail('id must be letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores')

178:     if (typeof finding[field] !== 'string' || finding[field].trim() === '') fail(`${field} must be a non-empty string`)

180:   if (!Array.isArray(finding.references) || finding.references.some(reference => typeof reference !== 'string')) {
181:     fail('references must be an array of strings')
182:   }
183:   const { file, line, endLine, snippet } = finding
184:   if (typeof file !== 'string' || file === '' || file.startsWith('/') || file.split('/').includes('..')) {
185:     fail('file must be a path relative to the target root')

187:   }
188:   const lines = target.linesOf(file)
189:   if (lines === undefined) {
190:     fail(`file ${file} is not in the tree under review`)
191:     return failures
192:   }
193:   if (!Number.isInteger(line) || line < 1 || line > lines.length) {
194:     fail(`line ${JSON.stringify(line)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
195:     return failures
196:   }
197:   const last = endLine === undefined ? line : endLine
198:   if (!Number.isInteger(last) || last < line || last > lines.length) {
199:     fail(`endLine ${JSON.stringify(endLine)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
200:     return failures
201:   }
202:   if (typeof snippet !== 'string' || snippet.trim() === '') {
203:     fail('snippet must quote the cited line')
204:     return failures
205:   }
206:   const quoted = normalize(lines.slice(line - 1, last).join('\n'))
207:   if (normalize(snippet) !== quoted) {
208:     fail(`snippet does not match ${file}:${line}, which reads ${JSON.stringify(quoted.slice(0, 160))}`)
209:   }
210:   return failures
211: }

213: /**
214:  * Read one findings file.
215:  * @param {string} path the file to read
216:  * @param {string[]} failures collector a malformed file is reported on
217:  * @returns {unknown[]} the entries, empty when the file is missing or malformed
218:  */
219: function readFindings(path, failures) {
220:   if (!existsSync(path)) {
221:     failures.push(`${path} is missing`)
222:     return []
223:   }

225:   try {
226:     parsed = JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, 'utf8'))
227:   } catch (error) {
228:     failures.push(`${path} is not JSON: ${error.message}`)
229:     return []
230:   }

238: /**
239:  * Decide one findings file on its own.
240:  * @param {string} path the findings file
241:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree it cites
242:  * @returns {{ failures: string[], invalid: string[], findings: unknown[] }} the broken rules, the ids that broke them, and the entries

245:   const failures = []

258: /**
259:  * The body of one section of the report.
260:  * @param {string} text the whole report
261:  * @param {string} heading the section heading, including its `##`
262:  * @returns {string} the text between this heading and the next one, empty when absent
263:  */
264: function section(text, heading) {
265:   const start = text.indexOf(`${heading}\n`)
266:   if (start === -1) return ''

272: /**
273:  * Decide SAFETY-REPORT.md, findings.json and the disclosure of what was dropped.

279:   const reportPath = join(root, 'SAFETY-REPORT.md')

291:   }

294:   const overclaim = OVERCLAIMS.exec(text)
295:   if (overclaim !== null) failures.push(`SAFETY-REPORT.md claims more than this review supports: ${JSON.stringify(overclaim[0])}`)

297:   const union = checkFindingsFile(join(root, 'findings.json'), target)

301:   const keys = new Set()

306:   }
307: 
308:   const listed = section(text, '## Findings')

311:   }

315:     if (!target.resolves(path, Number(line))) failures.push(`the citation ${path}:${line} does not resolve in the tree under review`)
316:   }
317: 
318:   const counts = Object.fromEntries(SEVERITIES.map(severity => [severity, findings.filter(finding => finding.severity === severity).length]))

320:     const body = section(text, heading)
321:     for (const severity of SEVERITIES) {
322:       const stated = new RegExp(`^- ${severity}: (\\d+)$`, 'm').exec(body)
323:       if (stated === null) failures.push(`${heading} does not state a "- ${severity}: <count>" line`)
324:       else if (Number(stated[1]) !== counts[severity]) {
325:         failures.push(`${heading} states ${severity}: ${stated[1]}, and findings.json holds ${counts[severity]}`)
326:       }
327:     }
328:   }
329: 
330:   const uncovered = section(text, '## What was not covered')
331:   const department = join(root, 'findings')
332:   const dropped = []
333:   if (existsSync(department)) {
334:     for (const entry of readdirSync(department).sort()) {
335:       if (!entry.endsWith('.json')) continue

346:   }

349:   if (!certificate.includes(HONESTY)) failures.push(`the Certificate must state, verbatim: ${JSON.stringify(HONESTY)}`)

lines.text: "title": "bcrypt-nodejs is unmaintained: last published in 2013, superseded by bcrypt/bcryptjs",

"evidence": "package.json pins bcrypt-nodejs at the exact version 0.0.3. `npm view bcrypt-nodejs time --json` (registry query run in this review) shows 0.0.3, published 2013-02-25, is still the latest version on the registry: the package has had no release, security or otherwise, in over 12 years. It carries no open npm-audit advisory today, but a password-hashing library with no maintainer response is a standing risk (CWE-1104): any future flaw in its bcrypt implementation will never be patched upstream.",

"impact": "No currently known CVE, so no immediate exploit; but the project's password hashing depends on a library nobody maintains, so any future vulnerability discovered in it (timing behavior, salt generation, native binding issues) has no upstream fix path and the application would carry it indefinitely.",
"fix": "Migrate to the actively maintained `bcrypt` (native binding) or `bcryptjs` (pure JS) packages, which receive continued security maintenance.",
"title": "body-parser range ^1.15.1 resolves to 1.18.3, vulnerable to two denial-of-service advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares body-parser ^1.15.1; package-lock.json resolves it to 1.18.3. `npm audit --json` run against the target's lockfile reports body-parser <1.20.3 as GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (high, CWE-405, denial of service when urlencoded parsing is enabled) and <1.20.6 as GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (low, CWE-770, invalid `limit` value silently disables size enforcement). Both ranges include the installed 1.18.3. body-parser is also a transitive dependency of the express install in this same tree, so the fix has to be applied consistently.",

"impact": "A request crafted to exploit the urlencoded-body parsing path can exhaust CPU or memory on the request-handling process, denying service to legitimate users of the whole NodeGoat app (every route uses body-parser via express.js).",
"fix": "Upgrade body-parser to >=1.20.6 (or adopt express's now-bundled body parsing on express 4.16+/5.x) and re-run `npm audit`.",
"title": "consolidate ^0.14.1 carries no current advisory but is templated around the also-abandoned swig engine",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves consolidate to 0.14.5; it does not appear in the 145-package npm-audit result, so no known CVE is currently open against it. It is listed for completeness because it is the module that wires the app to the abandoned `swig` template engine (see the swig finding on line 22); its own risk is tied to what it loads.",
"impact": "No standalone exploit path identified in this review.",
"fix": "No action required against consolidate itself; address it together with the swig replacement (see the swig finding).",
"title": "csurf is deprecated/archived upstream and pulls a vulnerable cookie parser",

"evidence": "package.json declares csurf ^1.8.3, resolved to 1.9.0 in the lockfile. `npm view csurf deprecated` (registry query run in this review) returns: 'This package is archived and no longer maintained.' `npm audit --json` flags the installed range (>=1.3.0) as low severity because it depends on `cookie` <0.7.0, GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x (CWE-74, cookie accepts name/path/domain values with out-of-bounds characters).",

"impact": "Low on its own (the cookie issue needs an application that trusts unsanitized cookie attribute values), but csurf being archived means no future CSRF-related fix will ever ship for it, and its underlying double-submit-cookie design has known bypasses documented by its own maintainers in the deprecation notice.",
"fix": "Replace csurf with a maintained CSRF middleware (e.g. `csrf-csrf` or a framework-level double-submit implementation) before its archived status becomes a liability.",
"title": "dont-sniff-mimetype has no open advisory but has seen no release since 2015",

"evidence": "Resolved to 1.0.0 in the lockfile; not present in the npm-audit vulnerability list. It sets the X-Content-Type-Options header, functionality now built directly into `helmet`, which this app also depends on, making the package redundant as well as stale.",
"impact": "No known exploit; functional overlap with helmet increases the dependency surface for no benefit.",
"fix": "Drop the dependency and rely on helmet's `noSniff()` middleware, which this app already installs.",
"title": "express range ^4.13.4 resolves to 4.16.4, an old 4.x with open XSS/open-redirect advisories and 10 transitive advisory-carrying packages",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves express to 4.16.4. `npm audit --json` reports the installed range (<=4.21.2) as high severity, naming GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx (low, CWE-79, XSS via response.redirect() for versions <4.20.0) and GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc (moderate, CWE-601/1286, open redirect on malformed URLs for versions <4.19.2); 4.16.4 falls in both vulnerable ranges. Walking the resolved dependency tree, express also pulls 10 other vulnerable packages (body-parser, cookie, debug, finalhandler, mime, ms, path-to-regexp, qs, send, serve-static), carrying 20 distinct advisories between them, several of which are independently listed as their own findings here (body-parser, cookie via csurf/express-session).",

"impact": "An attacker who controls part of a redirect target reachable through app.js's routes can produce a reflected-XSS payload or redirect a victim to an attacker-controlled site under the app's own domain, undermining any anti-phishing assumption users make about links from the app.",
"fix": "Upgrade express to at least 4.21.3, or move to the maintained 5.x line, then re-audit; this also picks up fixes in several of the ten transitively bundled packages.",
"title": "express-session ^1.13.0 resolves to 1.15.6 and bundles a vulnerable cookie parser and on-headers",

"evidence": "Resolved to 1.15.6. npm audit lists express-session's own advisory range (1.0.1-1.18.1) as low severity, inherited entirely from its two dependencies: `cookie` <0.7.0 (GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x, CWE-74) and `on-headers` <1.1.0 (GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q, CWE-241, HTTP response header manipulation). This is the middleware that issues NodeGoat's session cookie in app.js.",

"impact": "The on-headers flaw lets a value already under attacker influence manipulate response headers set through it, which for a session middleware means a path toward header-injection-based cookie or cache-control tampering on the session cookie itself.",
"fix": "Upgrade express-session to >=1.18.2 (pulls patched cookie and on-headers) and re-run npm audit to confirm the transitive advisories clear.",
"title": "forever ^2.0.0 resolves to 2.0.0 (2015-era), a critical-severity direct dependency carrying 35 additional vulnerable transitive packages",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves forever to 2.0.0. npm audit rates the installed range (>=0.7.4) critical and offers a fix only via a major upgrade to 4.0.3 (`npm view forever version` confirms 4.0.3 is the current published release, from 2022, so forever itself is still maintained upstream — this app is simply two majors behind). Walking forever's resolved subtree surfaces 35 further vulnerable packages beyond forever itself (nconf, flatiron, broadway, node-pre-gyp, tar, minimist, glob, semver, chokidar and others), 53 distinct GHSA advisories in total, several critical (e.g. GHSA-c2qf-rxjj-qqgw affecting bundled semver).",

"impact": "forever is a process supervisor listed under production `dependencies` (not devDependencies), so its vulnerable tree ships into whatever environment runs `npm install --production`; the specific advisories in its tree include ReDoS and prototype-pollution issues that are reachable if forever's CLI or any of its bundled tooling processes attacker-influenced input (e.g. config parsing via nconf/ini).",

"fix": "Upgrade to forever@4.0.3 (a breaking major-version change) or, if the goal is just process supervision in front of NodeGoat, replace it with a currently maintained process manager (e.g. pm2 or a systemd unit).",
"title": "helmet ^2.0.0 resolves to 2.3.0, six majors behind current (8.x), with a moderate configuration-override advisory in its bundled helmet-csp",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves helmet to 2.3.0; `npm view helmet version` shows the current release is 8.3.0. npm audit rates the installed range (0.3.0-3.20.1) high, driven by its dependencies `connect` and `helmet-csp`: GHSA-c3m8-x3cg-qm2c (moderate, Configuration Override in helmet-csp) plus debug's ReDoS advisories bundled via connect. Helmet is the security-headers middleware wired into app.js.",

"impact": "The helmet-csp configuration-override flaw can let a later helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() call, or a merged config object, silently weaken the CSP the app believes it is enforcing, undermining the app's main defense-in-depth control against injected scripts.",
"fix": "Upgrade to a current helmet major (8.x); the API changed significantly across majors 3-8, so this needs an app.js review of every `helmet.*()` call, not just a version bump.",
"title": "marked is pinned to the exact version 0.3.5, vulnerable to ReDoS and two XSS-sanitization bypasses",

"evidence": "package.json pins marked to the exact version 0.3.5 (no caret), matching what package-lock.json resolves. npm audit rates the installed range (<=4.0.9) high, listing six advisories that apply to 0.3.5 specifically: GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8 (XSS via data URIs, <0.3.7), GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc (HTML-entity sanitization bypass, <0.3.6), GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p (ReDoS, <0.3.9), GHSA-p9wx-2529-fp83 (ReDoS, <0.3.17), plus two later ReDoS advisories affecting everything before 4.0.10. This is the markdown renderer app/routes/memos.js uses to render user-submitted memo text (per the app's own tutorial content).",

"impact": "User-controlled markdown text rendered through marked 0.3.5 can carry a payload that bypasses its HTML-entity sanitization to achieve stored XSS, or a crafted input that triggers catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) and hangs the request-handling process.",

"fix": "Upgrade marked to a current 4.x+ release (fixArray reports 0.3.19 as the minimal same-major fix, but the ReDoS advisories are only fully closed at >=4.0.10), and re-verify any output-escaping assumptions memos.js makes.",
"title": "mongodb ^2.1.18 resolves to 2.2.36, a critical-severity driver bundling a bson deserialization flaw",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves mongodb to 2.2.36. npm audit rates the installed range (<=3.1.12) critical: mongodb's own advisory GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (high, denial of service, <3.1.13) applies, and its bundled `bson` <=1.1.3 carries GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr (critical, CWE-502, deserialization of untrusted data) plus GHSA-4jwp-vfvf-657p (moderate, same class); `mongodb-core` <=3.1.1 and `semver` are also flagged in the resolved subtree. This driver backs every DAO in app/data/*.js.",

"impact": "bson deserializing untrusted data at critical severity means any code path that decodes attacker-influenced BSON/BSON-like structures (or a crafted query response) risks memory corruption or unexpected object construction inside the driver, on top of the driver's own DoS advisory; the mongodb 2.x line is also 5 majors behind the currently supported driver, so it will not receive further security backports.",
"fix": "Upgrade the mongodb driver to a currently supported major (6.x or 7.x, matching your MongoDB server version), which is a breaking API change across every app/data/*.js file that uses it.",
"title": "needle is pinned to the exact version 2.2.4 and carries a moderate-severity ReDoS in its bundled debug dependency",

"evidence": "package.json pins needle to the exact version 2.2.4 (no caret), matched by the lockfile. needle itself has no direct advisory in the npm-audit output, but its dependency tree carries `debug` <4.3.1 (GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h, high, inefficient regex; GHSA-gxpj-cx7g-858c, low, ReDoS) and `ms`.",

"impact": "Low on its own; the debug ReDoS advisories require the debug namespace to log attacker-controlled strings, which is plausible but not confirmed for needle's specific use in this codebase.",
"fix": "Upgrade needle past 2.2.4 (a current 3.x release) to pick up a patched debug, or drop the exact pin so patch releases can flow through `npm audit fix`.",
"title": "node-esapi is an unfinished, single-release ESAPI port with no release since 2014",

"evidence": "package.json pins node-esapi to its only ever published version, 0.0.1. `npm view node-esapi time --json` (registry query run in this review) shows 0.0.1 published 2014-01-31 and still the latest: this is a 0.0.1 pre-release port of OWASP's ESAPI encoding/validation library that was never completed or maintained past its first publish. It is not in the npm-audit vulnerability list because no advisory has ever been filed against it, but a security-encoding library at version 0.0.1 with no subsequent release is not something to rely on for correctness.",

"impact": "Any encoding/validation routine the app calls through node-esapi runs unaudited, unmaintained code; a gap or bug in its encoder (there is no changelog to confirm coverage) would ship silently into the app's output-encoding path with no upstream fix ever coming.",

"fix": "Replace node-esapi with a maintained, actively-audited encoding library appropriate to the output context (e.g. the `he` package for HTML-entity encoding, or framework-level auto-escaping), and remove the ESAPI dependency once callers are migrated.",
"title": "serve-favicon ^2.3.0 resolves to 2.5.0 and pulls a moderate-severity ReDoS via ms",
"evidence": "Resolved to 2.5.0 in the lockfile. serve-favicon has no direct advisory in the npm-audit output; its dependency `ms` <2.0.0 carries GHSA-w9mr-4mfr-499f (moderate, ReDoS).",
"impact": "Low: ms's ReDoS requires attacker-controlled input to reach ms's time-string parser, which serve-favicon does not expose directly.",
"fix": "Upgrade serve-favicon to a release that pulls ms >=2.0.0, or run `npm audit fix`.",
"title": "swig ^1.4.2 is deprecated upstream with an unfixed critical arbitrary-file-read advisory",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves swig to 1.4.2, the last version swig's author ever published (`npm view swig time --json`, queried in this review, shows 1.4.2 published 2014-08-04 and still latest). `npm view swig deprecated` returns 'This package is no longer maintained.' npm audit rates the installed range (all versions, `*`) critical, naming GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (high, CWE-22, arbitrary local file read during template rendering) with `fixAvailable: false` — there is no patched version and there never will be. swig is one of the two template engines this app wires through `consolidate` (package.json line 10).",

"impact": "If any swig template path is influenced by user input (a template name, a partial/include path derived from a request parameter), an attacker can read arbitrary files off the server filesystem through the template-rendering path; and because no fix exists, this risk cannot be closed by upgrading.",

"fix": "Remove swig entirely and standardize on a maintained template engine already available in this stack (e.g. the other engine wired through consolidate), auditing every current .html template for swig-specific syntax that needs porting.",
"title": "underscore ^1.8.3 resolves to 1.9.1, inside the range vulnerable to critical arbitrary code execution via template()",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves underscore to 1.9.1. npm audit rates the installed range (<=1.13.7) critical: GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (critical, CWE-94, arbitrary code execution in underscore's `template()` function for versions >=1.3.2 <1.12.1) directly applies to 1.9.1, and GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (high, CWE-674/770, unbounded recursion in `_.flatten`/`_.isEqual`, <=1.13.7) also applies. `npm view underscore version` shows 1.13.8 is current and outside both vulnerable ranges.",

"impact": "If any code path passes a template string influenced by user input into underscore's `_.template()` (directly, or indirectly through another library that wraps it), an attacker gets arbitrary JavaScript execution on the server; the recursion issue separately allows a denial of service via a deeply nested or self-referential input to `_.flatten`/`_.isEqual`.",
"fix": "Upgrade underscore to >=1.13.8 and grep the codebase for any `_.template(` call sites to confirm none render request-controlled template strings.",
"title": "async ^2.0.0-rc.4 resolves to 2.6.1, inside the range vulnerable to prototype pollution",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves async to 2.6.1. npm audit rates the installed range (2.0.0-2.6.3) high, naming GHSA-fwr7-v2mv-hh25 (high, CWE-1321, prototype pollution, >=2.0.0 <2.6.4), which covers 2.6.1. `npm view async version` shows 3.2.6 is current, two majors ahead.",

"impact": "async is a devDependency used by the build/test tooling (not shipped to the running app), so the practical exposure is limited to whoever runs `npm run test`/CI on untrusted input; within that scope, prototype pollution in async can corrupt shared object prototypes and change the behavior of unrelated code running in the same process.",
"fix": "Upgrade async to >=3.2.6 (a breaking major change) or drop it if it's only pulled in transitively by other devDependencies.",
"title": "cross-env ^7.0.2 pulls a high-severity command-injection-adjacent flaw in cross-spawn",

"evidence": "Resolved to 7.0.2 exactly, no advisory against cross-env itself, but its dependency `cross-spawn` carries GHSA-3xgq-45jj-v275 (high, ReDoS in cross-spawn's command-line argument parsing).",

"impact": "cross-env only runs during `npm run dev`/local scripts, so exposure is limited to a developer's own machine processing an unusual argument list; not attacker-reachable from the deployed app.",
"fix": "Upgrade cross-env to a release that pulls a patched cross-spawn, or run `npm audit fix`.",
"title": "cypress ^3.3.1 resolves to 3.3.1, a critical-severity release 13 majors behind current, carrying 29 further vulnerable packages",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves cypress to 3.3.1. npm audit rates the installed range (0.1.0-15.15.0) critical with a fix only available at 16.1.0 (`npm view cypress version` confirms 16.1.0 is current). The resolved subtree carries 29 further vulnerable packages beyond cypress itself (request, tough-cookie, form-data, moment, lodash, qs, extract-zip, sshpk and others), 57 distinct advisories, several critical (e.g. lodash's GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 code injection via `_.template`, request's SSRF GHSA-jjv7-qpx3-h62q class of issues carried through its chain).",

"impact": "cypress is a devDependency used for e2e testing (test/e2e/*), not shipped with the running app, so this does not directly expose production traffic; the risk is to whoever runs the e2e/CI pipeline against untrusted fixtures or in a shared CI environment where the bundled request/lodash/tough-cookie flaws could be triggered by a malicious test fixture or a compromised CI dependency.",
"fix": "Upgrade cypress to the current major (16.x) as a dedicated migration, since the API and config format changed substantially since 3.x.",
"title": "grunt ^1.0.3 resolves to 1.0.3, vulnerable to arbitrary code execution, a race condition and path traversal",

"evidence": "package-lock.json resolves grunt to 1.0.3. npm audit rates the installed range (<=1.6.1) critical, naming GHSA-m5pj-vjjf-4m3h (high, CWE-1188, arbitrary code execution, <1.3.0), GHSA-rm36-94g8-835r (high, CWE-367, race condition, <1.5.3), and GHSA-j383-35pm-c5h4 (moderate, CWE-22, path traversal, <1.5.2) — all three ranges include 1.0.3. grunt drives this project's own build/test task runner (Gruntfile.js, `npm test`, `npm run db:seed`, `npm run precommit`). The resolved subtree also carries 16 further vulnerable packages (lodash, js-yaml, minimatch, glob, semver and others), 38 distinct advisories.",

"impact": "grunt runs locally and in CI to build/test/seed the database; the arbitrary-code-execution and path-traversal advisories mean a malicious Gruntfile task definition or a crafted file processed by an outdated grunt task could execute code or read files outside the intended project directory during a build or CI run.",
"fix": "Upgrade grunt to >=1.6.1 (npm audit reports a non-major fix is available) and re-run the full test/build pipeline.",
"title": "grunt-cli ^1.2.0 resolves to 1.3.2, inside the moderate-severity range via its liftoff dependency",

"evidence": "Resolved to 1.3.2. npm audit rates the installed range (1.3.0-1.3.2 || 1.4.1) moderate, inherited from `liftoff`; the resolved subtree separately carries 15 further vulnerable packages (debug, ini, micromatch, kind-of, set-value and the same brace-expansion/braces/fill-range chain seen under other grunt plugins), 13 distinct advisories.",
"impact": "grunt-cli is the CLI entry point for the build/test pipeline; its own moderate-severity advisory chain is limited to local/CI execution, not the deployed app.",
"fix": "Upgrade grunt-cli to >=1.5.0, which pulls a patched liftoff.",
"title": "grunt-env is declared as the floating range \"latest\" and its currently-resolved version pulls a critical lodash advisory",

"evidence": "package.json declares grunt-env as the literal string \"latest\" rather than a version or range — every `npm install` can resolve to whatever grunt-env's maintainers publish next, with no lockfile-enforced ceiling on what that pulls in. The lockfile currently resolves it to 1.0.1, which is not itself flagged, but its dependency `lodash` carries multiple advisories including GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 (high, code injection via `_.template`) and GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw (critical, prototype pollution), 11 distinct advisories across ini and lodash in total.",

"impact": "The floating \"latest\" declaration is itself a supply-chain exposure independent of today's resolved version (CWE-1357): a future grunt-env release could introduce new behavior or a new vulnerable dependency and it would install silently on the next `npm install` with no version bump to review in a diff.",
"fix": "Pin grunt-env to an explicit version (matching what package-lock.json currently resolves, or newer), and upgrade the lodash it pulls in.",
"title": "grunt-if is installed from a GitHub tarball pinned to the moving \"master\" branch, not a versioned registry release",

"evidence": "package.json points grunt-if at `https://github.com/binarymist/grunt-if/tarball/master` — a URL that resolves to whatever commit is HEAD on the `master` branch at install time, not a fixed, reviewable release (CWE-829, inclusion of functionality from an untrusted/unpinned control sphere). Separately, `npm view grunt-if version` shows the package's own last registry release was 0.1.5, published 2015-02-26 — over a decade with no update — and npm audit rates the resolved dependency (via grunt-contrib-jshint's own advisory chain) high severity; walking its resolved subtree surfaces 66 further vulnerable packages and 98 distinct advisories, several critical (grunt's own code-execution/path-traversal advisories, babel/istanbul chains, request's SSRF class issues).",

"impact": "Because the dependency is fetched from a mutable branch reference rather than a pinned tag/commit or a registry version, the exact code that lands in node_modules on any given `npm install` is not reproducible and not something the lockfile's integrity hash actually protects the way it does for registry packages: a compromise of that GitHub repository's master branch, or a maintainer force-push, changes what code every future install runs with no corresponding change to review in this project's own history.",

"fix": "Replace grunt-if with a maintained, registry-published alternative, or at minimum pin the tarball URL to an exact commit SHA and vendor/verify that commit's contents; either way, this is a decade-unmaintained micro-package that should be removed from the build.",
"title": "grunt-contrib-jshint ^3.0.0 resolves to 3.2.0 and pulls a high-severity ReDoS via its own bundled jshint",

"evidence": "Resolved to 3.2.0. npm audit rates the installed range (`*`, i.e. all published versions) high, inherited from its dependency `jshint`, itself vulnerable via `minimatch` (GHSA-hxm2-r34f-qmc5, high, CWE-400, ReDoS) and `shelljs` (GHSA-6c8f-qphg-qjgp/GHSA-952p-6rrq-rcjv, CWE-269, improper privilege management). npm audit reports no fix is available (`fixAvailable: false`) for grunt-contrib-jshint at its current major line.",
"impact": "Runs during local linting/CI only; a crafted source file processed by the vulnerable minimatch pattern matching could hang the lint task via catastrophic backtracking.",
"fix": "There is no in-range fix; either accept the risk for a CI-only tool with no attacker-reachable input, or replace grunt-contrib-jshint with a maintained ESLint-based grunt task.",
"title": "grunt-contrib-watch >=0.5.0 is flagged high severity and its resolved subtree carries 12 further vulnerable packages",

"evidence": "Resolved to 1.1.0. npm audit rates the installed range (>=0.5.0) high, with a fix only available via a major downgrade to 0.4.4 per its metadata — in practice this means using the current 1.1.0 release and upgrading its own dependency chain instead. The resolved subtree carries 12 further vulnerable packages (gaze, globule, websocket-driver, websocket-extensions, qs, debug, lodash and the same glob/minimatch/brace-expansion chain seen elsewhere), 34 distinct advisories.",

"impact": "grunt-contrib-watch runs a local filesystem watcher during development; its websocket-driver/websocket-extensions advisories matter if the dev server's live-reload channel is ever exposed beyond localhost.",

"fix": "Upgrade the dependencies grunt-contrib-watch pulls in (gaze, globule, websocket-driver) to their patched releases and re-audit; consider replacing it with `nodemon` (already a devDependency) for file-watching.",
"title": "grunt-npm-install bundles an old npm CLI with permission and arbitrary-file-write advisories",

"evidence": "Resolved to 0.3.1. npm audit rates its resolved range (`*`) moderate, entirely inherited from the bundled `npm` package it shells out through, which carries GHSA-c6rq-rjc2-86v2 (high, CWE-732, incorrect permission assignment for a critical resource), GHSA-hmw2-7cc7-3qxx (arbitrary file write, CWE-59/61), and GHSA-qrmc-fj45-qfc2 (symlink escape outside node_modules, CWE-22). npm audit reports no fix is available for grunt-npm-install itself (`fixAvailable: false`). "impact": "This grunt task shells out to run `npm install` as part of the build; the bundled npm's file-write/permission advisories could let a malicious package.json or a compromised transitive package escalate its install-time footprint (e.g. write outside node_modules) during that step.",
"fix": "Drop grunt-npm-install and run `npm install` directly as a build step (invoking the system's own current npm) instead of depending on a bundled, unpatched copy.",
"title": "grunt-retire — the task meant to catch outdated dependencies — is itself years out of date and pulls a critical advisory through its own `underscore` dependency",

"evidence": "Resolved to 0.3.12; `npm view grunt-retire version` shows 1.0.9 is current, and its own `retire` dependency in turn depends on `underscore`, which is independently flagged critical in this report (dep-underscore, GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq, arbitrary code execution) and on `request`, flagged for SSRF-class advisories (GHSA-jp4x-w63m-7wgm and related). npm audit rates grunt-retire's own resolved range (>=0.1.1) moderate.",

"impact": "The irony is functional as well as reputational: this project's own dependency-vulnerability scanner is running an outdated copy that shares the underscore/request risk it exists to catch, and cannot be trusted to have current advisory data at 0.3.12 either.",
"fix": "Upgrade grunt-retire to 1.0.9, or replace it with `npm audit`/`osv-scanner` run directly in CI, which is what this review used.",
"title": "jshint is pinned to the exact version 2.12.0 and carries a high-severity ReDoS via its bundled minimatch",

"evidence": "package.json pins jshint to the exact version 2.12.0 (no caret). npm audit rates the installed range (0.5.0 || >=0.6.0, i.e. effectively all releases) high, inherited from `minimatch` (GHSA-hxm2-r34f-qmc5, CWE-400, ReDoS) and `shelljs` (CWE-269, improper privilege management). `npm view jshint version` shows 2.13.6 is current. No fix is available in-range (`fixAvailable: false`).",

"impact": "jshint lints source files during CI/local development only; the ReDoS is reachable if a crafted source file's glob pattern matching hangs the lint step, a low-severity nuisance for a CI-only tool with no attacker-facing input in this app.",
"fix": "Upgrade jshint to 2.13.6, and remove the exact-version pin so future patch releases can flow through `npm audit fix`.",
"title": "mocha ^2.4.5 resolves to 2.5.3, inside the critical range because its bundled growl allows command injection",

"evidence": "Resolved to 2.5.3. npm audit rates the installed range (0.6.0-6.2.2) critical, driven by `growl` <1.10.0, GHSA-qh2h-chj9-jffq (critical, CWE-78/94, command injection in growl's desktop-notification shell-out). `npm view mocha version` shows 12.0.2 is current, ten majors ahead.",

"title": "nodemon ^1.19.1 resolves to 1.19.1, a high-severity release with 36 further vulnerable packages in its resolved subtree",

"title": "selenium-webdriver ^2.53.2 resolves to 2.53.3, pulling adm-zip's uncontrolled-memory-allocation and ws's memory-exhaustion advisories",

"evidence": "Resolved to 2.53.3. npm audit rates the installed range (2.43.1-4.0.0-rc-2) high, inherited from `adm-zip` <=0.6.0 (GHSA-xcpc-8h2w-3j85, high, CWE-400/789, crafted ZIP triggers 4GB allocation; GHSA-7q85-xj36-vmfc, high, uncontrolled memory allocation via declared size) and `xml2js` (GHSA-776f-qx25-q3cc, moderate, prototype pollution). `npm view selenium-webdriver version` shows 4.49.0 is current.",

"evidence": "Resolved to 0.2.0. npm audit rates the installed range (<=1.0.1) moderate at the package's own level, but its dependencies `lodash` (GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695, high, code injection via `_.template`; GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw, critical, prototype pollution) and `request` (GHSA-jp4x-w63m-7wgm and related, moderate SSRF-class issues) push the effective severity of running this tool to critical. `npm view zaproxy version` shows 2.0.0-rc.7 is current.",

33: ## Executive summary
34: 
35: This review covered NodeGoat, an intentionally vulnerable Express/MongoDB
36: application, over a locked tree of 111 files (sha256
37: 78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3), scoped to
38: authentication, session handling and authorization. Nine findings were kept, all
39: at `confirmed` confidence: zero critical, four high, five medium. The three most
40: important: (1) `POST /benefits` (app/routes/index.js:56) only checks that the
41: caller is logged in, never that they are an admin — the admin check exists but is
42: commented out — so any authenticated user can change any other user's benefit
43: start date; (2) `GET /allocations/:userId` (app/routes/index.js:63) loads a
44: user's allocation data straight from the URL parameter with no comparison to
45: `req.session.userId`, an unguarded direct object reference; (3) `addUser`
46: (app/data/user-dao.js:25) stores the signup password in plaintext, immediately
47: above the correct bcrypt-hashing code left in a comment. The method was to build
48: the full route table with its middleware chain first, then trace each kept
49: finding's source-to-sink path by reading the code; semgrep was used only to flag
50: lines worth reading, never as the finding itself. Third-party dependency
51: management, injection classes (SSJS eval, SSRF, ReDoS) and security headers/CSP
52: are out of this department's scope and are not covered here beyond what directly
53: touches authentication and sessions.
54: 
55: - critical: 0
56: - high: 4
57: - medium: 5
58: - low: 0
59: - info: 0
60: 
61: ## Scope and method
62: 
63: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat`, 111 files locked in `target.json`
64: (sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`), read
65: read-only. `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`; it was run with the local
66: `code-safety.yml` rule pack plus the registry pack `p/owasp-top-ten` (reachable,
67: so it was kept alongside the local rules), `--metrics off --json`, over the whole
68: target — 113 rules, 72 files scanned, 29 raw hits. None of the 29 hits were taken
69: as findings by themselves; each was read in context (the express-cookie-settings
70: hits on `server.js:78` corroborate the session-cookie finding below; the rest —
71: GitHub Actions mutable tags, `eval()` in contributions, an open redirect in
72: `/learn`, hardcoded config secrets, plaintext HTTP links in tutorial pages — are
73: real but outside this department's remit of auth/session/authorization and are
74: left to the injection/data/secrets/platform departments).
75: 
76: Files actually read line-by-line for this department: `server.js`,
77: `app/routes/index.js`, `app/routes/session.js`, `app/routes/profile.js`,
78: `app/routes/allocations.js`, `app/routes/benefits.js`,
79: `app/routes/contributions.js`, `app/routes/memos.js`, `app/routes/research.js`,
80: `app/routes/tutorial.js`, `app/data/user-dao.js`, `app/data/profile-dao.js`,
81: `app/data/benefits-dao.js`, `config/config.js`, `config/env/all.js`, and
82: `package.json` (checked for `csurf`, `helmet`, and any rate-limit dependency).
83: Method follows the department's `review-method` and `severity-and-evidence`
84: skills: every route and its middleware chain was enumerated first, then each kept
85: finding's tainted value was traced from the route registration through the
86: handler to its sink before being written down.
87: 
88: ## Findings
89: 
90: ### high
91: 
92: - `access-benefits-missing-admin-check` — `POST /benefits` lets any logged-in user modify any other user's benefit record with no admin check (`app/routes/index.js:56`, CWE-862, confirmed)
93: - `access-allocations-idor` — `GET /allocations/:userId` loads any user's allocation data by id with no ownership check (`app/routes/index.js:63`, CWE-639, confirmed)
94: - `access-plaintext-password-storage` — Signup stores the user's password in plaintext with no hashing (`app/data/user-dao.js:25`, CWE-916, confirmed)
95: - `access-csrf-missing-profile-update` — State-changing profile update (bank account, routing, SSN) has no CSRF protection (`app/routes/index.js:48`, CWE-352, confirmed)
96: 
97: ### medium
98: 
99: - `access-session-fixation-login` — Login handler does not regenerate the session id after authentication (session fixation) (`app/routes/session.js:116`, CWE-384, confirmed)
100: - `access-login-account-enumeration` — Login failure branches render different messages for an unknown user versus a wrong password (`app/routes/session.js:85`, CWE-204, confirmed)
101: - `access-weak-signup-password-policy` — Signup password validator accepts a single-character password (`app/routes/session.js:144`, CWE-521, confirmed)
102: - `access-login-no-rate-limit` — Login endpoint has no attempt limit, lockout or delay (`app/routes/index.js:34`, CWE-307, confirmed)
103: - `access-session-cookie-not-hardened` — Session cookie is issued with no Secure flag and no absolute expiry (`server.js:78`, CWE-613, confirmed)
104: 
105: ## What was not covered
106: 
107: - The tutorial pages under `app/views/tutorial/*.html` are NodeGoat's own lesson
108:   text and were read only to cross-reference the `isAdmin` fix comments; they were
109:   not treated as application attack surface.
110: - `app/routes/research.js`'s SSRF sink and `app/routes/contributions.js`'s
111:   `eval()` on request input were read (and flagged by semgrep) but are injection
112:   findings, not access findings, and are left to that department.
113: - `/login`'s account-lockout and rate-limit finding is scoped to the application
114:   code only; no deployment-level WAF, reverse-proxy, or cloud provider throttling
115:   was available to inspect, so this finding assumes none exists in front of the
116:   app as reviewed.
117: - JWTs are not used anywhere in this codebase (session-cookie auth throughout),
118:   so the JWT-pitfalls category of the `access` skill does not apply and was not
119:   checked further.
120: - MFA is not implemented anywhere in NodeGoat, so there is no MFA-bypass surface
121:   to evaluate; this is a gap in the product, not a specific line-level finding.
122: - Dependency-level vulnerabilities (the outdated `bcrypt-nodejs`, `swig`, and
123:   other packages in `package.json`/`package-lock.json`) are left to the

1: # Data department report — sensitive data exposure, logging and cryptography
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, read-only for this review).
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` printed `1.177.0`, so semgrep was run: `semgrep --config <local rules> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json .` from the target root. The registry pack (`p/owasp-top-ten`) was reachable; the run scanned 72 git-tracked files with 570+113 rules and produced 29 hits. Every hit was treated as a place to read, not as a finding on its own — semgrep flagged, among other things, `express-cookie-settings` on the session middleware in `server.js:78`, hardcoded-secret hits in `config/env/all.js:8`, `config/env/development.js:6` and `config/env/test.js:6`, and `plaintext-http-link` hits in two tutorial HTML pages. None of the raw semgrep hits are reported verbatim below; each candidate location was read in its surrounding function before being kept or dropped.
8: 
9: The review followed the entry points that handle sensitive data: the session/auth flow (`app/routes/session.js`, `app/data/user-dao.js`), the profile flow that collects SSN/DOB/bank details (`app/routes/profile.js`, `app/data/profile-dao.js`), the admin benefits flow (`app/routes/benefits.js`, `app/data/benefits-dao.js`), the config loader (`config/config.js`, `config/env/*.js`), the app bootstrap (`server.js`), the error handler (`app/routes/error.js`), and the database seed script (`artifacts/db-reset.js`). Views (`app/views/*.html`) were read wherever a route rendered a full DB document, to check what a template actually emits versus what reaches its rendering context.
10: 
11: ## Findings
12: 
13: Six findings, all in `findings/data.json`.
14: 
15: 1. **`data-http-cleartext-transport`** (high, confirmed, CWE-319) — `server.js:145` starts the app with `http.createServer(app).listen(...)`; the HTTPS alternative that would read `artifacts/cert/server.key`/`server.crt` is commented out. Every login, session cookie and profile submission crosses the network as cleartext.
16: 
17: 2. **`data-password-plaintext-storage`** (critical, confirmed, CWE-256) — `app/data/user-dao.js:25` stores the signup password verbatim; the `bcrypt.hashSync` call that would hash it (line 29) is commented out, and `validateLogin`'s comparison at line 61 is a raw `===` against the stored value, not `bcrypt.compareSync` (commented out at line 65). Every password in the `users` collection is recoverable in plaintext by anyone who reads the collection.
18: 
19: 3. **`data-pii-financial-plaintext-storage`** (critical, confirmed, CWE-311) — `app/data/profile-dao.js:61-66` writes `ssn` and `dob` (and, at lines 55-59, `bankAcc`/`bankRouting`) straight onto the document that gets `$set` into MongoDB. A working PBKDF2/AES encrypt-decrypt helper exists in the same file (lines 15-40) with its call sites (lines 67-76) but the whole block is commented out, so SSNs, dates of birth, and bank account/routing numbers sit in the database unencrypted.
20: 
21: 4. **`data-secrets-logged-at-startup`** (medium, confirmed, CWE-532) — `config/config.js:13` runs `console.log(util.inspect(config, false, null))` on the merged config object, which carries `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey` from `config/env/all.js:8-9` in plaintext. Every process start prints the session-signing secret and the AES key to stdout.
22: 
23: 5. **`data-seed-passwords-logged`** (medium, confirmed, CWE-532) — `artifacts/db-reset.js:99` logs `JSON.stringify(user)` for every seed user, including the plaintext `password` fields defined at lines 18, 27 and 35 (`Admin_123`, `User1_123`, `User2_123`).
24: 
25: 6. **`data-benefits-unprojected-pii-query`** (medium, likely, CWE-200) — `app/data/benefits-dao.js:16-20` queries `users.find({isAdmin:{$ne:true}})` with no projection, so full user documents (plaintext password, ssn, dob, bank details) flow into the `benefits` template's render context on every admin page load, even though the current `benefits.html` only prints `firstName`/`lastName`/`benefitStartDate`. Marked `likely` rather than `confirmed` because the current HTTP response body does not include the extra fields — the exposure is that they needlessly reach the render pipeline, not that the current template leaks them.
26: 
27: ## What was not covered
28: 
29: - **NoSQL injection paths** (`app/data/allocations-dao.js:73,78` `$where` usage flagged by the local semgrep rule, and the `eval()` calls in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`) were read only far enough to confirm they are not additionally a data-exposure sink; they are injection-department findings, not reported here.
30: - **SSRF in `app/routes/research.js:14-16`** (`needle.get(req.query.url + req.query.symbol)`) was noted but not analyzed further here — it is a request-forgery/injection concern, not a storage or logging one, though it could be used to reach internal HTTP services in cleartext.
31: - **Session cookie flags** (missing `secure`/`httpOnly`/`maxAge` on `server.js:78-102`) and **session fixation** (no `regenerate()` on login in `app/routes/session.js`) were read but left to the access/platform departments, per the department split in this review.
32: - **`config/env/all.js:8`'s hardcoded `cookieSecret`** as a secret-in-source-control finding is left to the secrets department; this report instead covers the separate fact that the same value (and `cryptoKey`) is also printed to stdout at every startup (`config/config.js:13`).
33: - **Dependency-level crypto weaknesses** (e.g. `bcrypt-nodejs` being an unmaintained package, per its own `package-lock.json` deprecation notice) were not assessed for CVEs; that is the dependencies department's remit.
34: - **Test/e2e fixtures** (`test/e2e/fixtures/users/*.json`, `test/security/profile-test.js`) were opened and contain only fixture/test credentials (e.g. `User1_123` used against a local Selenium/ZAP harness); not reported as findings since they are not production secrets, though `test/security/profile-test.js:37` does hardcode the same `User1_123` password checked in `artifacts/db-reset.js`.
35: - Runtime behavior this static read cannot confirm: whether a production deployment places a TLS-terminating reverse proxy in front of the plaintext `http.createServer` (nothing in this tree does so), and whether `NODE_ENV=production` (whose config file, `config/env/production.js`, is empty) changes any of the above at deploy time.
36: - No dynamic testing, dependency scanning beyond noting `bcrypt-nodejs`'s own deprecation notice, or infrastructure/deployment review was performed.

(End of file - total 36 lines)
</content>
